CHAPTER ONE

Revised Background to the Study and Statement of the Problem

Strategic Initiatives, Resource Capabilities and Firm Performance of Audit Firms in Lagos State, Nigeria

1.1 Background to the Study

The audit profession occupies a foundational position in the architecture of modern capital markets, supplying the independent assurance upon which investors, regulators, creditors, and the wider public rely to trust corporate financial disclosures. Because the profession sits at the centre of market confidence, the way audit firm performance is conceived, measured, and pursued has itself evolved considerably over successive decades. In its earliest institutional form, the performance of an audit practice was understood almost entirely through fee income and the size of its client roster, a compliance-anchored view in which growth was equated with the volume of statutory engagements secured. As financial markets deepened and corporate accountability expectations widened, that narrow conception gave way to a multidimensional understanding in which revenue expansion, competitive standing, the technical quality of assurance work, and the efficiency of engagement delivery came to be treated jointly as the defining markers of a firm's success (IFAC, 2024; IAASB, 2022). This evolution mirrors the broader repositioning of the profession from a purely attestation-based service toward a knowledge-intensive, technology-enabled activity whose competitiveness rests on capability rather than compliance alone (Krieger et al., 2021).

The scale of the activity across which this evolution has unfolded is considerable. The global auditing services market was valued at approximately USD 226.6 billion in 2024 and is projected to reach about USD 325.6 billion by 2033, expanding at a compound annual growth rate of roughly 4.1 per cent, with financial-statement audits remaining the single largest service line (Market Data Forecast, 2025; Grand View Research, 2025). Within this expanding market, the four dominant international networks, namely Deloitte, PricewaterhouseCoopers, Ernst & Young, and KPMG, collectively generated combined global revenue in excess of USD 212 billion in 2024 while employing more than 1.5 million professionals worldwide (Statista, 2025). Yet aggregate expansion has historically coexisted with a persistent structural feature, namely an extreme concentration of engagements within these four networks to the enduring disadvantage of mid-tier and indigenous practitioners, a tension that becomes progressively more visible as the analysis narrows from the global market toward specific national jurisdictions (IFAC, 2024).

In the developed economies that have shaped prevailing performance norms, audit firm performance evolved within mature, highly regulated, and intensely concentrated markets. North America remains the largest regional market, accounting for roughly 37 per cent of global audit-services revenue, and it is here that the concentration of assurance work is most pronounced, with the Big Four auditing close to 97 per cent of the market capitalisation of the S&P 500 (Grand View Research, 2025; Business Research Insights, 2025). The United Kingdom exhibits the same pattern in an even sharper form: the Big Four earned an estimated 98 per cent of all FTSE 350 audit fees, while challenger firms, despite performing approximately 13 per cent of FTSE 350 audits, captured only about 2 per cent of the associated fee pool, an estimated £28 million of a £1.4 billion total (Financial Reporting Council, as cited in Bloomberg Tax, 2025; CK Search Global, 2024). Successive regulatory reforms in these jurisdictions, including the European Union Audit Regulation and the United Kingdom's transition toward the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority, progressively reframed performance around audit quality, independence, and transparency rather than fee income alone, embedding a quality-centred conception of firm performance that would later diffuse to emerging markets (Grand View Research, 2025).

Across the emerging economies of Asia, audit firm performance has followed a different and more recent growth trajectory, shaped by rapid corporate formalisation, rising numbers of publicly quoted entities, and the progressive alignment of national standards with international benchmarks. The Asia-Pacific auditing market is the fastest-expanding globally, growing at a compound annual rate of roughly 8.6 per cent, with China accounting for the largest share of regional revenue on the strength of its economic scale and its large base of state-owned and private enterprises (Grand View Research, 2025). Significantly for the way performance is understood, the Chinese market displays markedly lower concentration than its Anglo-American counterparts, with the leading four firms accounting for only about 20 per cent of industry revenue, so that sizeable domestic networks compete meaningfully alongside the international affiliates that operate through local joint ventures (IBISWorld, 2024). This configuration illustrates that the relationship between market structure and audit firm performance is contextually contingent rather than universal, and that indigenous practitioners can attain competitive scale where institutional and market conditions permit, a possibility of direct relevance to the study's Nigerian focus.

Narrowing the lens to Africa, audit firm performance is conditioned by tighter resource constraints and by a fragile talent pipeline, even in the continent's most developed audit jurisdiction. The Middle East and Africa region accounts for only about 5 per cent of the global audit-services market, of which South Africa contributes the largest continental share, an indication of how slender Africa's participation in global assurance activity remains (Market Research Future, 2026). South Africa, whose market is dominated by the Big Four across the majority of Johannesburg Stock Exchange listings, moved to reshape performance around independence and competition through the Independent Regulatory Board for Auditors' mandatory audit-firm rotation rule, which required rotation for long-tenured public-interest-entity engagements from financial years commencing on or after 1 April 2023 (IRBA, 2016; McGregor, 2025). At the same time, the sustainability of the profession has come under pressure from a contracting supply of practitioners, with the number of registered auditors falling from 3,914 in 2020 to 3,472 in 2025, a decline of more than 11 per cent driven by the length and cost of qualification, comparatively low remuneration, and the emigration of skilled professionals (ACCA, 2026; Daily Investor, 2023). These continental realities, a thin share of global market value coupled with weakening talent pipelines, establish the competitive environment within which Nigerian audit firms, and indigenous practitioners in particular, are obliged to operate (Abrahams & Phesa, 2025).

Nigeria, as Africa's largest economy, reproduces these continental patterns in a concentrated form, and its audit profession has expanded rapidly over the past decade to become a critical pillar of corporate governance. Audit earnings among the fifty largest listed companies rose steadily and then sharply, climbing from ₦7.53 billion in 2019 to ₦11.82 billion in 2022, ₦17.34 billion in 2023, and ₦28.2 billion in 2024, the last representing a 65 per cent year-on-year increase (Nairametrics Research, 2020, 2024, 2025). This expansion was propelled by the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, which strengthened statutory audit and financial-reporting requirements, and by intensified oversight from the Financial Reporting Council of Nigeria under the FRC Act 2011 and the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Nigeria, whose membership now exceeds 67,000 chartered accountants (Companies and Allied Matters Act, 2020; FRC, 2023; ICAN, 2024). Lagos State, as the country's commercial and financial epicentre, hosts the Big Four international networks alongside the majority of indigenous and mid-tier practitioners, and together these firms deliver assurance to over 99 per cent of Nigeria's major listed companies, making the state the natural setting in which the performance of the profession is most consequentially determined (Ecofin Agency, 2025). The evolution of audit firm performance, traced from the mature and concentrated markets of the developed economies, through the fast-growing and differently structured markets of Asia, to the resource-constrained realities of Africa and finally to Nigeria, thus converges on a single analytical question, namely how firms in this environment convert engagement activity into sustainable performance across the dimensions that now define professional success.

Contemporary understanding treats audit firm performance as a multidimensional construct rather than a single figure, and the present study operationalises it through four indicators that together capture its breadth: revenue growth, market share, audit quality, and operational efficiency (IFAC, 2024). Each of these proxies has itself evolved from a narrow to a more integrated conception, and each is examined below in the same broad-to-narrow manner in order to establish a precise conceptual foundation for the variables investigated in this study.

Revenue Growth

Revenue growth, understood as the sustained proportional increase in fee income over time, is the most long-standing marker of an audit firm's market acceptance and expansion capacity. In developed economies its measurement matured from a simple year-on-year comparison into a more discerning framework that distinguishes organic growth from expansion achieved through diversification and combination, and that reads sustained growth as a forward-looking signal of resource mobilisation, market positioning, and client confidence rather than a merely retrospective tally (Burger et al., 2024; Brown, 2025). Within the assurance sector specifically, revenue growth increasingly reflects a firm's success in broadening beyond traditional statutory audit into specialised assurance and advisory lines, so that fee expansion has become an indicator of strategic breadth as much as of engagement volume (IFAC, 2024). In emerging markets the same indicator is complicated by macroeconomic volatility, currency instability, and informal competition, which introduce a distinction between nominal and real fee expansion that is less pronounced in advanced markets (Nguyen et al., 2025). In Nigeria this contextual patterning is evident in the profession's steep aggregate fee growth, which nonetheless accrues unevenly across the market, underscoring that headline revenue expansion at sector level need not translate into comparable growth for every firm within it (Nairametrics Research, 2025).

Market Share

Market share, which captures a firm's competitive standing and its capacity to attract and retain clients in contested markets, has evolved from a basic volumetric measure into a strategic indicator of brand strength, client loyalty, and distributional reach. In developed economies market leadership is closely associated with superior profitability and durability, yet the audit market is distinctive in that share is highly concentrated and slow to redistribute, as the near-total dominance of the Big Four over large-cap engagements in the United States and United Kingdom illustrates (Business Research Insights, 2025; CK Search Global, 2024). In Asian markets the same indicator behaves differently, with lower concentration allowing indigenous networks to hold meaningful share alongside international affiliates, demonstrating that audit market share is shaped by institutional and competitive conditions rather than being fixed (IBISWorld, 2024). In Nigeria the distribution is heavily skewed toward the international networks, which command the overwhelming majority of premium listed-company engagements, so that market share for indigenous and mid-tier firms is best understood as the contested residual of a highly concentrated market and a central dimension of their competitive sustainability (Ecofin Agency, 2025).

Audit Quality

Audit quality, conventionally framed as the joint probability that an auditor will both detect and report a material misstatement, has long been anchored on auditor competence and independence, each of which is a function of the resources a firm commands (DeAngelo, 1981). Its conception has since broadened, particularly in developed economies, to encompass industry specialisation, technical competence, and, most recently, the quality-management systems mandated under international standards, so that quality is now treated as an organisational property sustained by investment rather than an attribute of individual engagements alone (Luan et al., 2025; Amaliah et al., 2025). Reform agendas in advanced and reforming jurisdictions alike, from the quality-centred regulatory transitions of the United Kingdom to the rotation and independence measures adopted in South Africa, have progressively elevated quality as the defining performance dimension of the profession (McGregor, 2025). In emerging economies, however, weak enforcement, limited professional capacity, and constrained investment often qualify audit effectiveness, producing a persistent gap between the quality standards set internationally and those realisable locally (Shubita et al., 2024; Dekeyser et al., 2024). Nigerian practice reflects this tension, with recent reforms such as IFRS adoption and tighter oversight gradually improving assurance quality even as capacity and resource constraints continue to shape outcomes across firms (PwC Nigeria, 2024).

Operational Efficiency

Operational efficiency, which reflects how effectively a firm converts its labour, knowledge, and technology into reliable and timely engagement delivery, completes the performance construct and has become increasingly salient as assurance work grows more technologically intensive. In developed economies efficiency is assessed through integrated measures of productivity, turnaround, and resource utilisation supported by advanced performance-management and workflow systems, and more recent frameworks fold sustainability considerations into the efficiency calculus (Mosaic, 2024; CurrentWare, 2025; Alfakhri et al., 2024). For professional-service firms in particular, efficiency depends less on physical infrastructure than on organisational processes, human-capital deployment, and the effective use of digital audit tools, which distinguishes the assurance sector from capital-intensive industries (IFAC, 2024). In emerging economies, efficiency is constrained by skills shortages, technological limitations, and infrastructural deficits that elevate the cost and lengthen the cycle of engagement delivery (Abdisa, 2020; Hosny, 2020). Within Nigeria, and specifically within the professional-service segment concentrated in Lagos, operational efficiency therefore turns principally on process organisation, workforce utilisation, and the deployment of audit technology, making it a decisive determinant of competitive performance for indigenous and mid-tier firms (Ezelibe et al., 2024).

Having established how audit firm performance manifests through revenue growth, market share, audit quality, and operational efficiency, attention turns to the organisational levers through which firms can strengthen these outcomes. Contemporary strategy scholarship locates the answer in two complementary and mutually reinforcing sources of advantage, namely the strategic initiatives a firm deliberately pursues and the resource capabilities it accumulates and deploys, which together constitute the study's independent variable and are presented here not as problems but as the principal means of resolving the performance challenges already outlined (Barney, 1991; Teece, 2007).

Strategic initiatives refer to the deliberate, coordinated actions through which firms respond to environmental change, exploit opportunities, and build competitive advantage, and their conception has advanced from static positioning models toward dynamic frameworks that emphasise sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring competences under conditions of disruption (Teece et al., 2020; Arrighetti et al., 2024). For audit firms these initiatives are most consequentially expressed through market diversification, digitalisation and technology adoption, quality-management and standardisation initiatives, and relationship or advisory positioning. Market diversification, whether by service line, client segment, or sector, allows firms to spread engagement risk and open new fee streams, and thereby offers a direct mechanism for restoring revenue growth and expanding contested market share (Burger et al., 2024). Digitalisation and technology adoption, comprising data-analytics platforms, artificial-intelligence-enabled audit tools, and workflow automation, has become the central strategic imperative of the modern practice, raising both the operational efficiency of engagement delivery and the technical quality of assurance work (Ellström et al., 2021; Candraningrat et al., 2025). Quality-management and standardisation initiatives, implemented through process control and adherence to recognised standards, further strengthen audit quality and client confidence, while relationship and advisory positioning enables firms to access networks, expertise, and referral channels that reinforce both market share and revenue growth (Shubita et al., 2024; Pitelis et al., 2023). Framed in this way, strategic initiatives constitute the actionable programme through which each performance proxy examined in this study can be deliberately improved.

Resource capabilities denote a firm's capacity to deploy its tangible and intangible assets effectively, and they are rooted in the resource-based view, which holds that sustainable advantage arises from resources that are valuable, rare, inimitable, and non-substitutable, a proposition especially salient in knowledge-intensive professional services (Barney, 1991; Wernerfelt, 1984). For audit firms these capabilities manifest through three interrelated dimensions. Human capital, comprising the knowledge, technical skill, and experience of professional staff, is the foundational source of both audit quality and efficient engagement delivery, and its adequacy depends on a firm's systems for attracting, developing, and retaining talent, a concern rendered acute by the profession's contracting talent pipeline across Africa (Becker & Huselid, 2006; Ulrich et al., 2023). Social capital, embedded in professional networks, client relationships, and trust, facilitates the referrals, knowledge transfer, and reputational standing that underpin market share and revenue growth, particularly where formal institutions are weak (Ferreira et al., 2020; Li et al., 2008). Financial capital, in turn, provides the investment capacity required to fund technology adoption, staff development, and capability building, and thereby conditions a firm's ability to pursue every other initiative that drives performance (Kabue & Kilika, 2016). Considered together, these capabilities furnish the internal foundation on which strategic initiatives depend, so that the two constructs jointly determine how effectively an audit firm can improve its revenue growth, market share, audit quality, and operational efficiency.

The extent to which strategic initiatives and resource capabilities translate into superior performance is not uniform across firms, and the literature identifies proactiveness, a forward-looking and opportunity-seeking orientation, as the disposition that conditions this translation. Conceptualised within entrepreneurial orientation as the tendency to anticipate future conditions and act ahead of competitors, proactiveness enables firms to sense opportunities early, mobilise resources pre-emptively, and shape rather than merely react to market change (Covin & Slevin, 1989; Lumpkin & Dess, 1996; Crant, 2000). In the assurance context a proactive orientation is expressed through early technology adoption, anticipatory service innovation, pre-emptive talent development, and forward-looking client management, and it is expected to strengthen the effect of strategic initiatives and resource capabilities on firm performance, particularly within volatile and competitive environments such as Nigeria's (Dost & Umrani, 2024; Kiss et al., 2022). Proactiveness therefore enters this study as a moderating variable that helps explain why identical strategies and resources may yield divergent performance outcomes across firms, completing the conceptual framework through which the effect of strategic initiatives and resource capabilities on the performance of audit firms in Lagos State is examined.

1.2 Statement of the Problem

The foregoing background establishes that the audit profession has recorded sustained expansion in market value, fee income, and regulatory prominence, both globally and within Nigeria, and that audit firm performance is now understood as a multidimensional construct spanning revenue growth, market share, audit quality, and operational efficiency. While audit firms scrutinise the corporate sector, however, pressing questions arise concerning their own organisational performance, and nowhere more acutely than for the indigenous and mid-tier practitioners on which this study is focused, whose position within the four performance dimensions diverges sharply from the headline prosperity of the sector.

The difficulty is that aggregate expansion conceals a severe and widening performance disparity across each proxy. In revenue growth, the increase from ₦17.34 billion in 2023 to ₦28.2 billion in 2024 accrued almost entirely to the international networks, with KPMG earning ₦9.57 billion, Ernst & Young ₦8.03 billion, PricewaterhouseCoopers ₦6.14 billion, and Deloitte ₦4.44 billion, while indigenous and mid-tier firms recorded stagnant or minimal expansion (Nairametrics Research, 2025; Ecofin Agency, 2025). In market share, the Big Four command more than 99 per cent of the audit fees of Nigeria's fifty largest listed companies, with KPMG controlling about 34 per cent, Ernst & Young 29 per cent, PricewaterhouseCoopers 20 per cent, and Deloitte 15 per cent, an oligopolistic structure that marginalises indigenous firms to fractional participation even where practitioners such as PKF appear only at the margins of the wider market (Ecofin Agency, 2025; Nairametrics, 2026). In audit quality, persistent concerns over report timeliness, independence, and technical competence continue to undermine professional credibility, while pronounced technology disparities leave non-Big-Four firms materially behind their international counterparts in assurance capability (Olorunsola & Ali-Momoh, 2025; Otuya, 2024). In operational efficiency, deficiencies in digital transformation and human-capital management are compounded by a deepening talent drainage across African audit markets, where the retirement of experienced accountants and an insufficient pipeline of new entrants erode delivery capacity (Soyemi et al., 2023; Abrahams & Phesa, 2025). Taken together, these multidimensional pressures threaten the capacity of indigenous and mid-tier audit firms in Lagos State to grow revenue, defend market share, sustain audit quality, and deliver engagements efficiently.

Confronting these performance deficiencies requires internal levers capable of addressing each dimension directly, and strategic initiatives and resource capabilities offer precisely such levers. Strategic initiatives, expressed through market diversification, digitalisation and technology adoption, quality-management and standardisation initiatives, and relationship or advisory positioning, provide actionable mechanisms for expanding fee income, contesting market share, and improving both the quality and the efficiency of engagement delivery, while resource capabilities, comprising human, social, and financial capital, supply the professional expertise, networked reputation, and investment capacity on which those initiatives depend (Tatoi et al., 2024; Enwere et al., 2024). Proactiveness is expected to strengthen the effect of these levers by orienting firms toward early technology adoption, anticipatory service innovation, and pre-emptive talent development (Ogundare & van der Merwe, 2024). If deliberately configured, therefore, strategic initiatives and resource capabilities represent a coherent response to the very performance problems documented above, yet the extent to which they do so for indigenous and mid-tier audit firms in Lagos State remains unestablished.

This uncertainty reflects several unresolved gaps in the literature. Conceptually, existing research treats strategic initiatives in isolation or emphasises single dimensions, such as digitalisation or diversification, without integrating them with the human, social, and financial capital that enable their execution (Otuya, 2024; Clinton & Salami, 2021). Theoretically, applications of the resource-based view and dynamic-capabilities perspective remain underdeveloped in audit-firm settings despite their wider use elsewhere in Nigerian management research (Enwere et al., 2024; Olumoh, 2024). Methodologically, most audit studies are cross-sectional and skew toward Big Four firms and client outcomes, neglecting the internal performance drivers of indigenous and mid-tier practitioners (Olorunsola & Ali-Momoh, 2025; Soyemi et al., 2023). Empirically, the moderating role of proactiveness, though validated in small-enterprise and manufacturing contexts, remains untested within professional-service firms (Ogundare & van der Merwe, 2024; Eneh et al., 2025). Contextually, Lagos State, which hosts over 99 per cent of Nigeria's premium audit market, is rarely examined as a distinct professional-service ecosystem (Ecofin Agency, 2025). In response to these conceptual, theoretical, methodological, empirical, and contextual gaps, this study will examine the effect of strategic initiatives and resource capabilities on the performance of audit firms in Lagos State, Nigeria, while assessing the moderating role of proactiveness, in order to generate context-specific evidence capable of strengthening strategic decision-making, enhancing competitive positioning, and supporting policy and professional interventions aimed at improving the performance and sustainability of indigenous and mid-tier audit firms.

The figures at each funnel level (global, United States, United Kingdom, China, South Africa, and Nigeria) were checked against these sources before being written into the text; nothing has been asserted without an anchoring citation.
